components.label: US federal income tax

provenance.conversion: Official 2026 nominal thresholds are stored as real-dollar reference values under Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (published in IRB 2025-45); Social Security provisional-income thresholds remain nominal statutory amounts; open RMD bound uses null in canonical JSON.

components.scope: Ordinary brackets, standard deduction, LTCG stacking, Social Security provisional-income thresholds, RMD divisors, and early-withdrawal penalty.

components.label: Medicare IRMAA

provenance.conversion: CMS monthly Part B and Part D IRMAA surcharges are summed and multiplied by 12 into annual per-person surcharge tiers. The published intermediate thresholds are strict lower bounds for the next tier (an exact threshold remains in the preceding tier); the final $500,000 single/$750,000 MFJ threshold is inclusive for the top tier. The two-year MAGI lookback remains outside this refresh.

components.scope: Annual Part B and Part D surcharge tiers above the standard premium.

components.label: US contribution limits

provenance.conversion: First-year employee limits use 2026 IRS nominal limits; Rev. Proc. 2025-19 supplies the HSA amount; the 3% annual growth remains an explicit FIRE product modeling assumption, not an IRS value; HSA is the existing self-only modeled field and no family cap is modeled.

components.scope: First-year 401(k), Roth IRA, HSA limits and modeled annual limit growth.

components.label: ACA marketplace

provenance.conversion: 2026 Marketplace coverage retains the 2025 FPL basis used for the enrollment-year model; Rev. Proc. 2025-25 supplies the applicable-percentage reference. The existing 9.96% value is a flat proxy, not the full IRS piecewise schedule; it generally understates PTC below 300% FPL but can overstate it below 100% FPL because eligibility is not modeled. The 8.5% IRA value is a 2021-2025 historical counterfactual, not a current 2026 official value.

components.scope: Marketplace FPL basis, 400% cliff, and contribution-rate assumptions.

components.label: Social Security benefit rules

provenance.conversion: This component retains the existing FRA/claiming-age/delayed-credit rule inputs; FRA 67 and the 70%/100%/124% illustration apply to the 1960-and-later birth cohort, not all ages or older cohorts. The 2026 SSA fact sheet's 2.8% COLA belongs to the separate statement-import component and is payable in January 2026.

components.scope: FRA, claiming-age reduction, and delayed-retirement-credit rules.

components.label: SSA statement import

provenance.conversion: AWI remains capped at the latest official published 2024 series; the 2025 determination's 2.8% COLA is payable in January 2026. Future AWI values are not forecast.

components.scope: Local statement import AWI, COLA, and statutory bend-point derivation.

components.label: State income-tax archetypes (by type, not by state)
components.provenance: Assembled from published 2026 state rate schedules as TYPES. No row promises any particular state's law: rates are round representative values chosen to separate the archetypes, not to reproduce a filing.
components.scope: Representative state income-tax shapes by TYPE: ordinary and capital-gains rates, whether Social Security is taxed, and any retirement-income exemption. Never a particular state.

components.label: Social Security trust fund reserve depletion (OASI)

provenance.conversion: Depletion quarters are carried as the calendar YEAR in which reserves run out (2032 Q4 -> 2032), so a reduction begins in the year of depletion rather than the year after. The payable path is the intermediate alternative's two published endpoints -- 78 percent at depletion, 62 percent in 2100 -- and the straight line between them is THIS APP'S interpolation, not the report's; it is disclosed as such. The low-cost and high-cost alternatives contribute their depletion YEARS only: their payable percentages are not stated in the sources below and are recorded as null rather than guessed. DI reserves are projected positive throughout the 75-year period, so no DI depletion is modelled. The theoretical combined OASDI figures are carried for disclosure only and never reduce a benefit, because the law does not permit interfund borrowing and the app does not predict that it will.

components.scope: OASI reserve depletion timing and the share of scheduled benefits payable afterwards, under the Trustees' three published alternatives. Legislation is not projected.
components.source_vintage: 2026 OASDI Trustees Report (intermediate assumptions set February 2026)

components.label: US catch-up contributions and the annual additions cap

provenance.conversion: Nominal 2026 statutory dollar amounts, carried verbatim. The SECURE 2.0 higher catch-up applies to employees who ATTAIN age 60, 61, 62 or 63 during the year and REPLACES the age-50 amount for those years rather than adding to it; ages 64+ revert to the age-50 amount. The 415(c) figure is the employee-plus-employer annual additions cap and excludes catch-up contributions, which sit outside it. No family HSA cap and no 403(b)/457 special catch-ups are modelled.

components.scope: Age-50 and SECURE 2.0 age 60-63 catch-up amounts, IRA catch-up, and the section 415(c) annual additions limit.

components.label: US IRA income phase-out ranges

provenance.conversion: Nominal 2026 MAGI ranges, carried verbatim as [start, end] pairs. Contribution room falls linearly to zero across the range. The traditional-IRA ranges are DEDUCTION phase-outs and apply only to a taxpayer covered by a workplace plan; the Roth ranges are CONTRIBUTION phase-outs. Married-filing-separately (0 to 10,000 for both) is not carried because this engine models single and joint filers only.

components.scope: Roth IRA contribution and traditional IRA deduction MAGI phase-out ranges, single and married filing jointly.

components.label: US payroll tax (FICA): Social Security and Medicare

provenance.conversion: Employee-side rates only; the employer share is not a cost to the modelled household and is excluded. Pre-tax 401(k) and HSA deferrals do NOT reduce Social Security or Medicare wages, so FICA is charged on gross earnings. The 0.9 percent Additional Medicare threshold carried here is the FILING threshold (200,000 single / 250,000 joint), not the 200,000 employer WITHHOLDING trigger, which applies regardless of filing status; for a single filer the two coincide. Self-employment (SECA) rates are not modelled.

components.scope: Employee Social Security and Medicare rates, the Social Security wage base, and the Additional Medicare tax.

components.label: US self-employment tax (SECA)

provenance.conversion: SECA rates are the COMBINED employer and employee rates: 12.4 percent is 6.2 twice and 2.9 percent is 1.45 twice, which is why half of the bill is called the employer-equivalent portion. Both are applied to net earnings from self-employment, which is 92.35 percent of NET PROFIT (Schedule C / F / K-1) -- not of gross receipts and not of AGI. The Social Security component stops at the same wage base as employee FICA; the Medicare component does not stop. The deduction is 50 percent of the TOTAL SE tax, an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 line 15, and the 0.9 percent Additional Medicare Tax is NOT in that base -- it is computed separately on Form 8959, so it is neither halved nor deducted. The IRS self-employment topic page was NOT used for any dollar figure: it carries a stale 2024 wage base. The wage base and the Additional Medicare thresholds are not repeated here; they live in `fica_payroll_tax` and are read from there, so the two components cannot disagree.

components.scope: Self-employment tax rates, the net-earnings factor, and the deductible share, for tax year 2026.

components.label: US retirement plan shapes and HSA eligibility

provenance.conversion: Shipped ahead of the code that reads it, the same way the 415(c) cap was: a cited figure waiting in a dated pack is cheaper and safer than one recalled later. The engine now reads the 401(a)(17), SEP/self-employed rate conversion, SIMPLE base and age catch-up limits, and governmental 457(b) deferral limit; the 403(b) special catch-up and HSA/HDHP fields are now read by their product contracts. Four things a naive reading gets wrong. (1) The SEP percentage is 25 percent for a common-law EMPLOYEE but 20 percent for a SELF-EMPLOYED person, because their own contribution reduces the compensation it is computed on: rate / (1 + rate) = 0.25 / 1.25. (2) The 403(b) 15-year catch-up is the LEAST of three amounts and is applied BEFORE the age-50 catch-up, and the two are additive. (3) The 457(b) special final-three-years catch-up CANNOT be combined with the age-50 catch-up in the same year. (4) A 457(b) limit is SEPARATE from the 401(k)/403(b) limit, so a person with both may defer the full amount to each; 403(b) and 401(k) instead SHARE one 402(g) limit. DELIBERATELY ABSENT: the separate SECURE 2.0 higher-tier SIMPLE catch-up tied to the enhanced small-employer tier. The higher DEFERRAL tier (18,100) is published for 2026 and is here; the ordinary SIMPLE age-50 catch-up (4,000) and age-60-through-63 catch-up (5,250) are also here and are now read by the engine. A distinct enhanced-tier catch-up figure is not recorded; the 3,850 that circulates is the 2025 amount. Recording it as a 2026 figure would be the exact mistake this pack exists to prevent. ADDED 2026-08-24 (OPEN_ITEMS E37): deferral_limit_457b_governmental, the section 457(e)(15) elective deferral limit for 2026, 24500 (from 23500 in 2025) per Notice 2025-67. It is recorded SEPARATELY even though it equals the 402(g) figure this year, because point (4) above is what makes it worth having: they are two limits that happen to coincide in 2026, and a reader who reused the 401(k) constant would silently lose that the day they diverge.

components.scope: Plan-shape contribution limits (403(b), 457(b), SEP, SIMPLE), the annual compensation limit, and HSA/HDHP eligibility thresholds.

components.label: Section 423 employee stock purchase plan limits

provenance.conversion: The 25000 limit is measured at grant-date fair market value for each calendar year in which the option is outstanding, not at payroll deductions or purchase-date value. The 0.15 rate is the maximum discount implied by the statutory floor of 85 percent of the lesser of grant-date or exercise-date fair market value. This product's first contract supports annual same-calendar-year grant and purchase offerings only; multi-year option accrual is not collapsed into this annual ceiling.

components.scope: Section 423 annual grant-date fair-market-value ceiling and maximum purchase discount for annual offerings.
